unit.title: Ser vs. Estar — the meaning shift
unit.subtitle: Adjectives that change meaning with ser or estar

grammar.title: Same adjective, two completely different meanings
grammar.intro: At C1 the ser/estar contrast stops being about ‘permanent vs. temporary’ and becomes lexical: many adjectives literally change meaning depending on the verb. Ser listo means clever, but estar listo means ready; ser rico means wealthy, but estar rico means tasty. Getting these wrong is one of the clearest tells of a non-native speaker.

sections.heading: The classic meaning-shift adjectives
sections.body: With these adjectives, ser marks an inherent trait or identity, while estar marks a condition, state or perception. The English translation changes completely:

ex.es: Juan es muy listo, pero todavía no está listo.
ex.en: Juan is very clever, but he isn't ready yet.

ex.es: La tarta está riquísima, aunque su familia es rica.
ex.en: The cake is delicious, though his family is wealthy.

sections.heading: More pairs that trip people up
sections.body: The same logic runs through a whole set of adjectives. Note that estar bueno means tasty (and, colloquially, good-looking), never simply ‘to be a good person’:

ex.es: Todavía está verde para dirigir el proyecto.
ex.en: He's still too green to lead the project.

ex.es: Estoy orgulloso de ti, aunque él es muy orgulloso.
ex.en: I'm proud of you, though he is very arrogant.

sections.heading: ser vs. estar + past participle
sections.body: With a past participle the contrast is aspectual: ser + participle is the true passive (it names the action, often with por), while estar + participle describes the resulting state after the action is over:

ex.es: La puerta fue cerrada por el guardia a las diez.
ex.en: The door was closed by the guard at ten.

ex.es: Cuando llegué, la puerta ya estaba cerrada.
ex.en: When I arrived, the door was already closed.

takeaways: Same adjective, different verb, different meaning: es listo (clever) vs. está listo (ready).
estar rico = tasty; ser rico = wealthy. estar malo = ill; ser malo = a bad person.
estar verde = unripe/not ready; ser verde = inexperienced. estar orgulloso = proud; ser orgulloso = arrogant.
ser + participle = the passive action (often + por); estar + participle = the resulting state.

mistakes.why: To say food tastes good, use estar: está rica. Ser rica here would mean the food is ‘wealthy’.

mistakes.w: Hoy soy malo, no voy a trabajar.
mistakes.r: Hoy estoy malo, no voy a trabajar.
mistakes.why: To be ill is estar malo; ser malo means to be a bad or evil person.

mistakes.w: Estoy muy orgulloso; nunca pide ayuda a nadie.
mistakes.r: Es muy orgulloso; nunca pide ayuda a nadie.
mistakes.why: As a permanent character trait (arrogant) use ser orgulloso; estar orgulloso means proud of something.

exercises.prompt: Ese crío ___ listísimo: capta cualquier concepto al vuelo.
exercises.prompt_en: That kid is really clever: he grasps any concept instantly.
exercises.no: ‘Clever’ as a trait is ser listo; está listo would mean he's ‘ready’.

exercises.prompt_en: —Shall we go now? —Yes, I'm ready now.
exercises.no: ‘Ready’ is estar listo; soy listo would mean ‘I'm clever’.
For taste, use estar: “Esta paella está riquísima.”

exercises.prompt: No vino a trabajar porque ___ malo toda la semana.
exercises.prompt_en: He didn't come to work because he was ill all week.
exercises.hint: ‘To be ill’ = estar malo (past tense here).
exercises.no: ‘To be ill’ is estar malo → estaba malo. Ser malo would mean ‘evil’.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression to its meaning.

exercises.no: It was: “El plátano todavía está verde.” (still unripe → estar verde).

exercises.scenario: A friend tells you she passed a tough civil-service exam 🎓

lines.speaker: Lucía
lines.en: I finally passed the civil-service exam!

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Estar orgulloso de alguien = feeling proud.
exercises.no: To feel proud of someone is estar orgulloso; ser orgulloso means arrogant.

exercises.en: He didn't come because he was ill.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the sound of “No vino porque estaba malo.”
